<reason>While Side B presented an eloquent case centered on shifting the burden of legislative inertia, Side A won by out-executing on institutional mechanics and failure modes. Side A neutralized the problem of legislative silence via minority-triggered privileged revocation votes, exposed how fast-track rules still cannot prevent substantive midnight hostage-taking by swing factions under a sunset deadline, and devastated Side B's attempt to write off a 24-hour lapse of emergency powers as a harmless "day of argument." Side A also won the judicial review clash by showing that panicked legislative renewals certify the ongoing existence of an emergency and insulate stale executive overreach from court intervention.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's response in [A4.1]-[A4.4] to Side B's fast-track question and "next day" defense: Side A cleanly distinguished procedural obstruction from substantive hostage-taking by swing votes at a deadline, then showed why even a 24-hour lapse in banking backstops, quarantines, or wartime authorities triggers irreversible legal and operational chaos.</best_rebuttal>
